hints: Think about what makes any $\text{O-H}$ acid strong: how stable is the negative ion left behind after $\text{H}^{+}$ is lost?
Compare where the lone pair or negative charge can go in $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COO}^{-}$, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}^{-}$ and $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}^{-}$.
Consider how the $\text{C=O}$ group pulls electrons compared with the $\text{CH}_{2}$ group which pushes electrons toward the $\text{O-H}$ bond.
walkthrough:
Set the order from anion stability**
Picture each acid losing $\text{H}^{+}$. You get $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COO}^{-}$, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}^{-}$ and $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}^{-}$. The more spread out and stabilised that minus charge is, the more easily the $\text{H}^{+}$ is lost, so the stronger the acid. That logic gives benzoic acid strongest, then phenol, then phenylmethanol weakest.

See why benzoate is best stabilised**
In benzoic acid the $\text{C=O}$ group is strongly electron withdrawing by negative inductive effect, which pulls electron density away and weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond. Once $\text{H}^{+}$ leaves, the minus charge is delocalised equally over the two oxygen atoms of $\text{COO}^{-}$. That delocalisation is very stabilising.

See why phenoxide is intermediate**
In phenol the lone pair on the $\text{OH}$ oxygen overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. This delocalisation pulls electron density away from O and weakens the $\text{O-H}$ bond. The phenoxide ion $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}^{-}$ is stabilised by delocalisation into the ring, but less effectively than the carboxylate ion, so phenol is weaker than benzoic acid.

See why phenylmethanol is weakest**
In $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$ the $\text{CH}_{2}$ group sits between the ring and the $\text{OH}$. It cannot delocalise the lone pair into the ring. Instead alkyl groups donate electrons by positive inductive effect, pushing electron density onto O and strengthening the $\text{O-H}$ bond. The anion $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{O}^{-}$ is localised and not stabilised, so it is essentially a normal alcohol, least acidic.

Final answer: benzoic acid ($\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH}$) most acidic > phenol ($\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$) > phenylmethanol ($\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{OH}$) least acidic.
Any two of: benzoic acid has negative inductive effect of $\text{C=O}$ which weakens $\text{O-H}$ and carboxylate negative charge is delocalised over two O atoms, stabilising the anion; phenol lone pair on O is delocalised into benzene ring which weakens $\text{O-H}$; phenylmethanol has positive inductive effect of $\text{CH}_{2}$ which strengthens $\text{O-H}$.

hints: Recall that $\text{Na}$ reacts with any $\text{O-H}$ group to give $\text{H}_{2}$, even very weak acids like alcohols.
Recall that $\text{NaOH}$ neutralises carboxylic acids and phenols, but not typical alcohols.
Recall that only acids stronger than carbonic acid ($\text{H}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$) liberate $\text{CO}_{2}$ from $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$, so compare with the order from (a).
walkthrough:
Sort by reagent strength**
Think of the three reagents as tests of increasing acid strength needed. $\text{Na}$ is the least selective, it gives $\text{H}_{2}$ with carboxylic acids, phenols and alcohols. $\text{NaOH}$ needs a moderately acidic proton. $\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$ needs a fairly strong acid to release $\text{CO}_{2}$.

Apply Na to all three**
All three compounds contain an $\text{O-H}$ group: $2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_{2}$. So benzoic acid, phenylmethanol and phenol all give effervescence of $\text{H}_{2}$ with $\text{Na(s)}$. Three ticks in the top row.

Apply NaOH**
Benzoic acid is neutralised: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COONa} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Phenol is just acidic enough: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{ONa} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Phenylmethanol as an alcohol is too weak to react. So tick, cross, tick.

Apply Na2CO3**
Only an acid stronger than carbonic acid will give $\text{CO}_{2}$: $2\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH} + \text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3} \rightarrow 2\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COONa} + \text{CO}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Phenol ($K_a$ about $10^{-10}$) and alcohols are weaker than $\text{H}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}$, so no reaction. So tick, cross, cross.

Final answer: $\text{Na(s)}$: benzoic acid ✓, phenylmethanol ✓, phenol ✓
$\text{NaOH(aq)}$: benzoic acid ✓, phenylmethanol ✘, phenol ✓
$\text{Na}_{2}\text{CO}_{3}\text{(aq)}$: benzoic acid ✓, phenylmethanol ✘, phenol ✘

hints: Write the standard equations for $\text{RCOOH} + \text{PCl}_{5}$ and $\text{RCOOH} + \text{SOCl}_{2}$ and balance Cl, P, S and O atoms.
walkthrough:
Recall the two classic chlorinating reagents**
Replacing $\text{OH}$ by $\text{Cl}$ with $\text{PCl}_{5}$ always gives $\text{POCl}_{3} + \text{HCl}$ alongside $\text{RCOCl}$. With $\text{SOCl}_{2}$ you get $\text{SO}_{2} + \text{HCl}$ alongside $\text{RCOCl}$. Balancing gives: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH} + \text{PCl}_{5} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCl} + \text{POCl}_{3} + \text{HCl}$ and $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH} + \text{SOCl}_{2} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCl} + \text{SO}_{2} + \text{HCl}$.

Final answer: reaction 1: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH} + \text{PCl}_{5} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCl} + \text{POCl}_{3} + \text{HCl}$
reaction 2: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH} + \text{SOCl}_{2} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCl} + \text{SO}_{2} + \text{HCl}$

hints: Compare the physical states of $\text{POCl}_{3}$ versus $\text{SO}_{2}$ and $\text{HCl}$ and think which mixture is easier to separate from liquid $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCl}$.
walkthrough:
Link state to separation**
$\text{POCl}_{3}$ is a liquid that stays mixed with liquid benzoyl chloride and needs fractional distillation. In contrast $\text{SO}_{2}$ and $\text{HCl}$ are both gases that bubble out of the reaction mixture by themselves. With no liquid by-products left behind, the $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCl}$ is already pure.
Final answer: In reaction 2 all by-products, $\text{SO}_{2}$ and $\text{HCl}$, are gaseous and escape, leaving pure $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCl}$ with no liquid by-products to separate.

hints: Identify the electrophile as the $\delta^{+}$ carbon of $\text{C=O}$ in $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCl}$ and the nucleophile as a lone pair on O in $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.
Remember the first step forms a tetrahedral intermediate with $\text{OH}_{2}^{+}$, $\text{O}^{-}$ and $\text{Cl}$ all attached to the same carbon.
Think about which lone pair reforms the $\text{C=O}$ in the second step and which bond must break to expel the leaving group.
Check that every curly arrow starts from a lone pair or bond and points to an atom or bond, with correct $\delta^{+}$ on C, $\delta^{-}$ on O, and formal charges shown.
walkthrough:
Set up the electrophile and nucleophile**
Look at $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{C(=O)Cl}$. Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so label $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$. That $\delta^{+}$ carbon attached to electron withdrawing $\text{Cl}$ is strongly electrophilic. Water provides the nucleophile through one of its two lone pairs on O.

Draw the addition step**
Draw a curly arrow from the lone pair on O of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to the $\delta^{+}$ C of the $\text{C=O}$. At the same time draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond up onto the O to give $\text{O}^{-}$. This forms the tetrahedral intermediate where the central C is bonded to $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}$, $\text{Cl}$, $\text{OH}_{2}^{+}$ and $\text{O}^{-}$: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{C(OH}_{2}^{+})(\text{O}^{-})\text{Cl}$.

Draw the elimination step**
Now the $\text{O}^{-}$ lone pair pushes back to reform $\text{C=O}$. Show this with a curly arrow from the $\text{O}^{-}$ lone pair to the $\text{C-O}$ bond. As the double bond reforms, the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond must leave. Show this with a curly arrow from the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond to $\text{Cl}$, giving $\text{Cl}^{-}$.

Check charges and arrows**
Make sure you have shown: lone pair on attacking water, $\delta^{+}$ on C and $\delta^{-}$ on O, arrow O to C, arrow $\text{C=O}$ to O, correct intermediate charges ($+$ on $\text{OH}_{2}$, minus on O), arrow $\text{O}^{-}$ to reform $\text{C=O}$, arrow $\text{C-Cl}$ to $\text{Cl}$. Subsequent proton transfers then give $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COOH} + \text{HCl}$.

Final answer: Mechanism: lone pair on O of $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ attacks $\delta^{+}$ C of $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$ in $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCl}$; $\pi$ bond of $\text{C=O}$ breaks to O; tetrahedral intermediate $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{C(OH}_{2}^{+})(\text{O}^{-})\text{Cl}$ formed; lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ reforms $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-Cl}$ bond breaks to $\text{Cl}^{-}$.

hints: Recall the two stage name for nucleophilic attack on an acyl chloride to give a tetrahedral intermediate followed by loss of $\text{Cl}^{-}$.
walkthrough:
Name the two stages**
Water first adds to the $\text{C=O}$ to make the tetrahedral intermediate, then $\text{HCl}$ is eliminated as $\text{C=O}$ reforms. This is nucleophilic addition followed by elimination, so the mechanism is addition-elimination.
Final answer: addition-elimination (nucleophilic addition-elimination)

hints: Use Fig. 5.1 to see that each anhydride $\text{-CO-O-CO-}$ comes from one $\text{-COCl}$ plus one $\text{-COO}^{-}\text{Na}^{+}$.
Split the repeat unit in Fig. 5.2 at the anhydride $\text{C-O-C}$ bonds to find a bis(acyl chloride) fragment and a dicarboxylate fragment.
walkthrough:
Apply the Fig. 5.1 pattern to the polymer**
Fig. 5.1 shows $\text{R-COCl} + \text{R'-COONa} \rightarrow \text{R-CO-O-CO-R'} + \text{NaCl}$. So every $\text{-CO-O-CO-}$ linkage in the polyanhydride is made from a $\text{COCl}$ end and a $\text{COONa}$ end. To find monomers, cut the polymer at those anhydride O bridges.

Identify the two complementary monomers**
Cutting Fig. 5.2 at the $\text{-CO-O-CO-}$ gives two possibilities that are chemically equivalent. One monomer provides the long aromatic diether part and the other provides the succinyl part. Either the aromatic part is the diacyl chloride $\text{ClOC-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-COCl}$ with sodium succinate $\text{NaOOC-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-COONa}$, or the reverse: aromatic dicarboxylate $\text{NaOOC-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-COONa}$ with succinyl chloride $\text{ClOC-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-COCl}$.

Final answer: $\text{ClOC-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-COCl}$ and $\text{NaOOC-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-COONa}$
OR $\text{NaOOC-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-O-C}_{6}\text{H}_{4}\text{-COONa}$ and $\text{ClOC-CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{-COCl}$

hints: Think which small molecule in the environment can break an anhydride $\text{-CO-O-CO-}$ back to two carboxylic acids, as in (d).
walkthrough:
Link anhydride reactivity to degradation**
You saw in (d) that $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{COCl}$ and by analogy acid anhydrides are readily attacked by water. In soil or in the body, water hydrolyses the anhydride links $\text{-CO-O-CO- + H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{-COOH}$, breaking the chain into small diacid molecules. Dilute acid or alkali speeds this hydrolysis.
Final answer: hydrolysis (by water, or heating with dilute aqueous acid or alkali)
